newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Shipley sees good reasons for ECNZ break-up.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Shipley sees good reasons for ECNZ break-up.

text.p: State-Owned Enterprises Minister Jenny Shipley on Wednesday said there were good reasons for splitting state energy company ECNZ in a way that would leave generators close to their markets.

"I have a view on the future structure of the energy market, and it is clear that if you have generators close to where the demand is, that you are more likely able to price the cost of power accurately," Shipley told parliament's finance and expenditure select committee.
"One of the things that ECNZ is faced with is generating capacity that stretches across a wide chunk of New Zealand," Shipley said.

"I think as you look at the concept of energy sources, the transmission lines in terms of (national grid operator) Transpower and demand, then pockets of generating capacity either existing or new (emerge)...then there is a good argument to the break up of ECNZ," she said.
She said she thought one of the most interesting questions was whether a break-up should be into two or three companies.
The government announced in the June budget it would review the shape of the energy market. Prime Minister Jim Bolger has since said it is almost certain ECNZ would be split.
In June 1995 Contact Energy, controlling about 29 percent of the country's generating capacity, was split from ECNZ and a cap of 75 percent of total capacity was put on ECNZ.
Shipley said she had preliminary discussions with the board of ECNZ on the future shape of the company.

"There is no question ECNZ would prefer to be left alone and indeed they would love to have the cap of no more than 75 percent of generator capacity taken off them," Shipley said, adding the board wanted to grow the business.

"We equally want the energy market to develop to its maximum efficiency in the interest of the consumers, so we are having to balance up those two objectives. I have every confidence the existing board will facilitate the study and the conclusion, or the anticipated conclusion, that there will be a break up of ECNZ."
But she said she expected ECNZ to "wheel and deal" over whether in return it could be allowed to expand its generation.
"You can describe it fairly as an active negotiation'," Shipley said.
